analysis.one_liner: Rewrites Medicare's exceptions to the ban on doctors profiting from their own patient referrals.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two House subcommittees in August 1995 and never received a vote before the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicare generally forbids doctors from referring patients for services to businesses they own or get paid by, because a doctor with a financial stake has an incentive to order more care. This bill would rewrite the exceptions to that ban: it would let doctors who share a building bill Medicare for services furnished through their shared facility, expand the exception for services done in a doctor's office to cover medical equipment and nutrition supplies, create an exception for insurance arrangements where doctors are paid a fixed amount per patient, and require that payments between doctors and health businesses be in writing, at fair market value, and not tied to referral volume. It would also remove eyeglasses, contact lenses, and lens implants for cataract surgery from the ban entirely.
analysis.who_benefits: Physicians with ownership stakes or payment arrangements with health care businesses, and the suppliers of equipment and eye-care products they refer patients to. The shared-facility and in-office equipment exceptions would let doctors profit from services they themselves order, and the eye-care exclusion would lift the ban from eyeglasses, contacts, and lens implants. The uniform written, fair-market-value payment rules would also give physicians and their business partners clearer, more predictable ground rules than the existing list of narrow exceptions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Physicians with stakes in health businesses

how_it_helps.text: Creates a new exception letting physicians in the same building share a facility, furnish services to their own patients, and bill Medicare for them [S3].
Expands the in-office services exception to cover durable medical equipment and nutrients, equipment, and supplies, so doctors can bill for equipment used in their offices [S3].
Adds an exception for capitated payment arrangements, where a physician group is paid a fixed per-patient amount and bears the financial risk, which supports managed-care style arrangements [S3].

Replaces the patchwork of narrow exceptions for payment arrangements with a single set of requirements: the deal must be in writing, signed, at fair market value, not tied to referral volume, commercially reasonable, and limited to necessary services [S3].

Removes intraocular lenses, eyeglasses, and contact lenses from the list of services covered by the referral ban, freeing eye doctors from conflict-of-interest restrictions on those products [S3] [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Medicare and its beneficiaries. Research on physician self-referral has found that doctors who own the facilities they refer to tend to order more services, and each new exception widens the set of services a doctor can profit from ordering, with the cost falling on the Medicare program and taxpayers. Beneficiaries also lose a protection when eyeglasses, contacts, and lens implants are pulled out from under the ban.

drawbacks.text: The new exceptions let doctors profit from services they order for their own patients. Physician ownership of referral targets has been associated with higher utilization and higher Medicare spending, so each exception added here shifts more of that business back into doctors' hands [S3].

Excluding eyeglasses, contact lenses, and intraocular lenses from the referral ban removes all conflict-of-interest limits on doctors selling or referring for those products, including lens implants during cataract surgery [S3] [S2].

The fair-market-value requirement cuts both ways: while it bars pay tied to referral volume, it also legitimizes a wide range of physician-business payment arrangements that meet the six written tests, giving physicians a clearer path into deals with entities they refer to [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill has a genuine defense: the existing ban's list of narrow exceptions was widely criticized as confusing, and a single clear set of fair-market-value rules for payment arrangements could reduce accidental violations. But the substance tilts toward expansion — new exceptions for shared facilities, in-office equipment, and capitated payments, plus a full carve-out for eye-care products, all widen the channel through which doctors can profit from care they order. The clarity gains are real; so is the loosening.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in two House subcommittees after its August 1995 referral and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 104th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on August 2, 1995, and referred to the Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee [S1] [S5].
Within two weeks it was sent to the Health subcommittee of Commerce and the Health and Environment subcommittee of Ways and Means [S5].
No further action was ever recorded; the bill died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing self-referral ban and its exception list stayed exactly as they were. Physicians and suppliers with ownership arrangements got neither the new exceptions nor the revised payment rules, and Medicare beneficiaries kept the protections they had.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was a senior California Democrat with a single Republican cosponsor; there were no votes and no recorded opposition, so no partisan pattern is visible in the record.

industries.note: The bill creates new exceptions letting doctors bill Medicare for services furnished through shared facilities, in-office equipment, and capitated arrangements — businesses they own or are paid by and refer their own patients to. Because self-referral is associated with ordering more services, the gain to doctors comes largely at Medicare's expense.

Bringing durable medical equipment and nutrition supplies under the in-office ancillary exception would let physician-owned suppliers sell equipment billed to Medicare without triggering the referral ban.

Excluding eyeglasses, contact lenses, and intraocular lenses from designated health services removes the only conflict-of-interest restriction on physicians selling or steering patients to these products, including lenses implanted during cataract surgery.

industries.industry: Hospitals and health businesses paying physicians
industries.note: The bill requires every compensation arrangement to be written, at fair market value, and untied to referral volume, which constrains some arrangements — but meeting those six requirements would give businesses a clear, predictable safe harbor for paying physicians.
